batiment.resume: The Building itself — Ulam, Heikhal and Kodesh HaKodashim under one roof. Seen from the front, from the east, it is a square block 100 amot wide and 100 high, roughly 48 by 48 meters. But the body that stands behind the vestibule is only 70 amot wide: “narrow behind and wide in front, like a lion.” The Ulam therefore overhangs by 15 amot on each side, and these two overhangs were called Beit HaChalifot: the knives were stored there. The exterior is not gilded: it is the stone itself, white, green and blue marble in alternating courses, one projecting, one recessed.
cotes: façade 100 amot wide × 100 high (≈ 48 × 48 m)
rear body 70 amot wide
the Ulam overhangs by 15 amot on each side
total east-west length 100 amot: wall of the Ulam 5, Ulam 11, wall of the Heikhal 6, Heikhal 40, Amah Traksin 1, Kodesh HaKodashim 20, wall 6, cell 6, wall 5
elevation: foundation 6, interior height 40, ceiling and decoration 5, upper floor 40, roof 5, Ma'ake 3, Kaleh Orev 1 — total 100

sources.citation: narrow behind and wide in front, like a lion
שֶׁכָּל הַבַּיִת טוּחַ בְּזָהָב, חוּץ מֵאַחַר הַדְּלָתוֹת
אַפֵּיק שָׂפָה וְעַיֵּיל שָׂפָה
וּמְיֻסָּד אֲבָנִים יְקָרוֹת אֲבָנִים גְּדֹלוֹת אַבְנֵי עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת וְאַבְנֵי שְׁמֹנֶה אַמּוֹת

batiment.note: Adopted: the façade is not gilded — Herod wanted to overlay it with gold, and he was advised to leave the stone visible, as it “looks like the waves of the sea” (Bava Batra 4a; Sukkah 51b); the gold is inside (Middot 4:1). Adopted: the three marbles of the second version in Bava Batra 4a, “בְּאַבְנֵי כּוּחְלָא, שִׁישָׁא וּמַרְמְרָא”; according to Rabba there were only two, without the blue. Set aside: R. Yehuda (Middot 4:6), for whom the Kaleh Orev does not count in the height and the Ma'ake is four amot. Tour's choice: masonry of blocks sawn smooth, on the model of Shlomo's buildings (I Kings 7:9-10), where the stones of ten and eight amot are those of the foundations.

oulam.resume: The vestibule, the first room of the Building as one comes from the courtyard. It is very wide and shallow: only 11 amot from east to west, but 90 from north to south between its walls (100 overall), since it overhangs the body of the Temple by 15 amot on each side. Its façade is banded, not flat: rovadim, horizontal projecting ledges, gird it from bottom to top — one ama of bare wall, then a projecting band three amot high, the topmost one four amot high. No column, no pilaster, no pediment: all the articulation given by the sources is horizontal.
cotes: 11 amot deep (east-west) × 100 wide
wall of the Ulam 5 amot
overhang of 15 amot on each side (Beit HaChalifot)
rovadim: 1 ama bare, band 3 amot high, the upper rovad 4 amot

sources.citation: כֹּתֶל הָאוּלָם חָמֵשׁ, וְהָאוּלָם אַחַד עָשָׂר… הָאוּלָם עוֹדֵף עָלָיו חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה מִן הַצָּפוֹן, וַחֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה מִן הַדָּרוֹם
עֳבִי כֹּתֶל הָאוּלָם חָמֵשׁ אַמּוֹת
וְכֵן סָבִיב לְכָתְלֵי הָאוּלָם מִלְּמַטָּה עַד לְמַעְלָה… אַמָּה אַחַת חָלָק וְרֹבֶד שָׁלֹשׁ אַמּוֹת… וְרֹבֶד הָעֶלְיוֹן הָיָה רָחְבּוֹ אַרְבַּע

oulam.note: Adopted: no column or pilaster on the façade; no source places any in front of it (Middot 3:7-8 and 4:6-7, Rambam). Yakhin and Boaz, from the First Temple (I Kings 7:21), stand inside the Ulam, on either side of the opening. The tour's reading: the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 4:9) alternates “מִלְּמַטָּה עַד לְמַעְלָה” one bare ama and a rovad of three amot, of which he gives the “רֹחַב” (width); the tour takes these three amot as the height of the band. Tour's choice: the projection of the bands, which no source gives, set at one ama.

douze_marches_oulam.nom: The Twelve Steps of the Ulam
douze_marches_oulam.resume: Between the floor of the Azara and the threshold of the Ulam, twelve steps. Each rises half an ama; the tread is one ama, but Middot 3:6 inserts landings of three amot and gives the top one four, so that, by Bartenura's reckoning, they occupy nineteen of the twenty-two amot separating the altar from the Ulam; the three amot on the altar side are level paving. This is where the Kohanim go up to stand and bless the people — on the steps, not in the courtyard.
cotes: twelve steps
each step: ½ ama high, 1 ama of tread, except three landings of 3, 3 and 4 amot
they occupy 19 of the 22 amot between the Ulam and the Mizbeach

sources.citation: בָּאוּ וְעָמְדוּ עַל מַעֲלוֹת הָאוּלָם
נִמְצְאוּ כָּל הַמַּעֲלוֹת תְּשַׁע עֶשְׂרֵה אַמּוֹת מִן הָרִאשׁוֹנָה עַד הָאוּלָם

douze_marches_oulam.note: Adopted: the first opinion in Middot 3:6, a top landing of four amot. Set aside: R. Yehuda (Middot 3:6), who gives it five; the steps then begin two amot from the altar (Bartenura).

petah_oulam.resume: The opening of the Ulam: 40 amot high by 20 wide, and without a door — the Ulam had none. According to Ketubot 106a and the Rambam (Klei HaMikdash 7:17), a curtain nonetheless hung at this entrance. Above the opening run five gall-oak beams, the maltera'ot, of increasing length, separated from one another by courses of stone; Bartenura describes them as painted and ornamented. Through this opening passes the gaze of the Kohen who, from the top of the Mount of Olives, sees the entrance of the Heikhal over the eastern wall, lower than the others.
cotes: opening 40 amot high × 20 wide
five gall-oak beams (maltera'ot) of increasing length
without doors

אַחַת לְפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל הֵיכָל, וְאַחַת לְפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם

petah_oulam.note: Tour's choice: the curtain at the entrance is not shown, so that the interior can be seen from the courtyard.

gefen_zahav.resume: A golden vine suspended on posts above the entrance of the Heikhal, at the back of the Ulam. It was not fixed: leaves and clusters that people offered were added to it.

couronne_helene.resume: A golden lamp, the nivreshet, offered by Queen Helena and placed above the entrance of the Heikhal. It reflected the rising sun.

sources.citation: הִילְנִי אִמּוֹ עָשְׂתָה נִבְרֶשֶׁת שֶׁל זָהָב עַל פִּתְחוֹ שֶׁל הֵיכָל

couronne_helene.note: Tour's choice: the shape of the lamp and the way it hangs; Yoma 3:10 only places it “עַל פִּתְחוֹ שֶׁל הֵיכָל”.

sharsherot_oulam.nom: The Golden Chains of the Ulam
sharsherot_oulam.resume: Golden chains fixed in the beams of the ceiling of the Ulam and hanging in the air. Young Kohanim would grab hold of them and climb, to go see the crowns that Zechariah has kept “as a memorial in the Sanctuary.” Bartenura places these crowns at the windows of the Heikhal — they are not modeled here.

sources.citation: וְשַׁרְשְׁרוֹת שֶׁל זָהָב הָיוּ קְבוּעוֹת בְּתִקְרַת הָאוּלָם, שֶׁבָּהֶן פִּרְחֵי כְהֻנָּה עוֹלִין וְרוֹאִין אֶת הָעֲטָרֹת

ותולות למטה באולם שאוחזין בהן פרחי כהונה מפסגין ועולין

tables_oulam.nom: The Two Tables of the Ulam
tables_oulam.resume: Two tables stand in the Ulam, near the entrance of the Heikhal. One is of marble: on it are placed the fresh loaves about to go in. The other is of gold: it receives the loaves that come out.
cotes: two tables: one of marble, one of gold

heikhal.resume: The Holy Place: a hall 40 amot from east to west, 20 from north to south, and 40 high — roughly 19 meters by 9.6, under a 19-meter ceiling. It is tall and narrow, almost a nave. Walls and ceiling are gold-plated; the coffered cedar ceiling and the gold floor are taken from the First Temple. Light comes from windows that Rashi describes as narrow on the inside and wide on the outside, so that they send light out rather than take it in. Walking westward, one has the Table on the right, in the north, and the Menora on the left, in the south.
cotes: interior 40 amot (east-west) × 20 (north-south) × 40 high (≈ 19 × 9.6 × 19 m)
wall of the Heikhal 6 amot

sources.citation: שֶׁכָּל הַבַּיִת טוּחַ בְּזָהָב, חוּץ מֵאַחַר הַדְּלָתוֹת
transparent within, sealed without: I have no need of light
וַיִּסְפֹּן אֶת הַבַּיִת גֵּבִים וּשְׂדֵרֹת בָּאֲרָזִים
וְאֶת קַרְקַע הַבַּיִת צִפָּה זָהָב לִפְנִימָה וְלַחִיצוֹן
צר שבחלון היו מבפנים והרוחב שבחלון מוחזר כלפי חוץ להוציא אורה לעולם

heikhal.note: First Temple: the cedar ceiling (I Kings 6:9), the gold floor (I Kings 6:30) and the windows (I Kings 6:4, discussed in Menachot 86b); Middot 4:1 speaks only of gold. Yet the Rambam writes “וְאֵין בּוֹנִין בּוֹ עֵץ בּוֹלֵט כְּלָל” (Beit HaBechirah 1:9), which weighs against an exposed wooden ceiling: the cedar is the tour's choice.

portes_heikhal.resume: The entrance of the Heikhal measures 20 amot high by 10 wide and has four doors: two outer and two inner. Their gold plating is taken from the First Temple. In front of the entrance, Ketubot 106a and the Rambam (Klei HaMikdash 7:17) further place a curtain, an outer parokhet. During the avoda the doors are open, the outer leaves folded back into the thickness of the embrasure, the inner ones into the Heikhal, against the wall.
cotes: entrance 20 amot high × 10 wide
four doors (two outer, two inner)
embrasure of 6 amot

אַחַת לְפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל הֵיכָל
וְאַחַת עַל פֶּתַח הַהֵיכָל
וּשְׁתֵּי דַלְתוֹת עֲצֵי בְרוֹשִׁים… וְצִפָּה זָהָב מְיֻשָּׁר עַל הַמְּחֻקֶּה

portes_heikhal.note: Tour's choice: the four doors are shown open, as during the service, and the curtain is not shown. First Temple: I Kings 6:34–35; Middot 4:1 does not say what the doors were made of. Set aside: R. Yehuda (Middot 4:1), for whom the doors stood within the embrasure and folded back on themselves.

taim.resume: Thirty-eight cells arranged over three floors gird the Heikhal and the Kodesh HaKodashim: fifteen to the north, fifteen to the south, eight to the west, connected to one another by openings. At the northeast corner, a turning ramp, the Messiba, rises toward the upper floor and the roofs of the cells; to the south, a strip three amot wide bears the name Beit Horadat HaMayim, “the house of the descent of the water.” Above the Heikhal and the Kodesh HaKodashim lies the upper floor, the Aliyah: hatches there open onto the Kodesh HaKodashim, through which workers were lowered in closed crates when it needed repair.
cotes: 38 cells: 15 to the north, 15 to the south, 8 to the west
north and south: five over five, and five above; west: three over three, and two above
the cell widens floor by floor: 5, then 6, then 7
the wall of the Heikhal recedes by one ama at each floor: 7, then 6, then 5 (tour's choice)
the six of wall and six of cell in Middot 4:7 taken as the middle floor (tour's choice)
three openings per cell: to the right, to the left, and toward the one above

taim.note: Tour's choice: the height of each story of cells, their length and the thickness of the walls between them — the sources do not give them. Adopted: Rashi's reading, reported by Tosafot Yom Tov (Middot 4:4) — the widths in Middot 4:4 are those of the cells, and the recesses are cut into the wall of the Heikhal; the 7, 6 and 5 of that wall, which make the breakdown of Middot 4:7 the middle floor, are the tour's choice. Set aside: Bartenura and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 4:9), for whom these 5, 6 and 7 are galleries (yetzi'im) outside the wall of the Messiba, and it is that wall that recedes.

mesiba.resume: The turning ramp that rises from the northeast corner up to the door of the upper floor. One went up facing west, went the whole length of the north face to the west, turned south, went the whole length of the west face, then turned east, and walked along the south to the door of the upper floor, which opens to the south. It was also by this ramp that one went up onto the roofs of the cells.
cotes: 3 amot wide, its wall 5, in the north strip
a single circuit: north, then west, then south
to the south, in the 3-ama strip that Middot 4:7 names Beit Horadat HaMayim (tour's choice)

arrival at the level of the floor of the upper story, 51 amot above the pavement: otem 6, ground floor 40, flooring 5 (Middot 4:6), the otem counted from the pavement of the Azara (tour's calculation)

mesiba.note: Tour's choice: Middot 4:7 reserves a strip for the Messiba only on the north; on the south, the three amot are the Beit Horadat HaMayim, and on the west it counts none. Middot 4:5 nonetheless runs the ramp along the west and the south: the tour cuts the west corridor into the thickness of the cell wall and runs the south ramp in the strip of the Beit Horadat HaMayim, up to the door of the upper floor. The slope and height of the corridor, which no source gives, are also choices.

aliyah.resume: The upper floor of the building: forty amot of clear height above the Heikhal and the Kodesh HaKodashim, separated from the ground floor by five amot of flooring. This is not an attic — it is a room one enters: its door opens to the south, at the end of the Messiba, and two cedar poles are planted there to climb onto its roof. A line of markers replays on the floor the separation below between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, and hatches cut into the floor open onto the Kodesh HaKodashim: workers were lowered through them in closed crates, so that they would not feast their eyes on the Holy of Holies.
cotes: 40 amot high, from 51 to 91 above the pavement of the Azara
five amot of flooring: one ama of kiyour, two of beit dilfa left empty (according to the Rambam), one ama of tikra, one ama of maaziva
the same five amot above, then the Ma'ake (3) and the Kaleh Orev (1)
door to the south, at the end of the Messiba
two cedar poles at this door, for the roof

הַקּוֹרוֹת הָעֶלְיוֹנוֹת… הָיָה עָבְיָן שְׁתֵּי אַמּוֹת, וְהֵן קְרוּיִין בֵּית דִּלְפָה
מִקַּרְקָעִית הַבַּיִת עַד קֵרוּי עֲלִיָּה רִאשׁוֹנָה שְׁלֹשִׁים אַמּוֹת, וּמֵעֲלִיָּה לַעֲלִיָּה עַד גַּג הָעֶלְיוֹן תִּשְׁעִים אַמּוֹת
והקרוב אצלי כי האולם לבדו היה לו זה הגבה, ובו היו העליות

aliyah.note: Adopted: the upper floor is above the Heikhal and the Kodesh HaKodashim, where Middot 4:5 describes it and where Rashi puts the upper stories of the First Temple (on II Chronicles 3:4). Set aside: Radak's reading (ibid.), which places them in the Ulam, while noting that the Sages also put upper stories above the Heikhal; above the Ulam, the tour leaves the building solid. Adopted: the empty beit dilfa of the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 4:3), “פָּנוּי שֶׁיִּכָּנֵס בּוֹ הַדֶּלֶף”. Set aside: Bartenura (Middot 4:6), for whom these are the upper beams, two amot thick. Tour's choice: two hatches of two amot on the axis — no source gives their number or position.

kaleh_orev.resume: The very last half-meter of the building: an ama of iron at the ridge, to keep birds from landing there. The Rambam describes it in place — an iron band one ama high that girds the Heikhal above the parapet on its four sides, sharp as a sword, so that no bird lands on it, its feet being cut off. A continuous blade, then, and not a row of spikes. The hundred amot of height are not a hundred amot of wall: the masonry stops at 96, and the last four amot are the parapet, for three, and this anti-crow device, for one.
cotes: 1 ama
the wall stops at 96 amot; the last 4 are the Ma'ake (3) and the Kaleh Orev (1)

sources.citation: בְּחֶשֶׁק שֶׁל בַּרְזֶל גֹּבַהּ אַמָּה חַד כְּמוֹ הַסַּיִף

kaleh_orev.note: Adopted: the anonymous view of the mishna (Middot 4:6) — a parapet of three amot and a kaleh orev of one ama. Set aside: R. Yehuda, for whom the kaleh orev is not counted in the hundred amot and the parapet is four amot.

maake.resume: The parapet that lines the roof of the building, three amot above the wall, which itself stops at 96 amot. Its perimeter is not a rectangle: it steps in at the plane of the wall of the Heikhal, since the Ulam overhangs by 15 amot on each side.

maake.note: Adopted: the anonymous view of the mishna (Middot 4:6) — a parapet of three amot and a kaleh orev of one ama. Set aside: R. Yehuda, for whom the parapet is four amot and the kaleh orev is not counted.

menora.resume: The pure gold candelabrum, hammered from a single piece, stands to the south of the Heikhal, two and a half amot from the wall, facing the Table. It is 18 tefachim high, that is three amot, about 1.44 meters. Seven branches, in a single plane oriented north-south according to R. Elazar b. R. Shimon and the Rambam, adorned with 22 cups, 11 knobs and 9 flowers, on a base with three feet. Hollow, as the halakha allows, it weighs a kikar of gold with its lamps, about 58 kilograms. The six lamps of the branches turn their spouts toward the middle one, whose spout faces the Kodesh HaKodashim. In front of it, three stone steps, for the Kohen who comes to trim the wicks; between the two stages of that work, he leaves the kuz, a large gold pitcher, on the second step. Its seven flames are the only warm light in the room.

menora.note: Adopted: the lamps aligned north to south, with R. Elazar b. R. Shimon (Menachot 98b) and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 3:12). Set aside: Rabbi, for whom the Menora stood east to west (Menachot 98b). Adopted: straight branches rising on a diagonal, following the Rambam's drawing (Commentary on the Mishna, Menachot 3:7) and Rashi (on Exodus 25:32). Set aside: the rounded branches of common depictions. Adopted: the cups upside down, mouth downward, as in the Rambam's drawing. His commentary nonetheless describes the cup as narrow at the bottom, and warns that the drawing does not show its exact form, only the number and placement of the ornaments (Rambam on Menachot 3:7).

shulchan.resume: The Table stands to the north of the Heikhal, two and a half amot from the wall, in the western half of the room, facing the Menora. It measures 2 amot long, 1 wide, 1.5 high, in acacia wood gold-plated, with a rim, the zer. It bears the twelve showbreads, the Lechem HaPanim, arranged in two stacks of six that rise about two amot above it. The loaves are separated by 28 gold tubes, carried by four gold uprights set on the floor, which extend past the stacks and rise higher than the Menora. In the tour, two incense cups are set on the stacks; the Rambam places them beside the stacks.

shulchan.note: Adopted: the western half of the Heikhal, beyond twenty amot from the entrance. Menachot 98b reconciles “half” and “a third” of the building: the third is counted over the 60 amot of the Heikhal and the Kodesh HaKodashim. Adopted: R. Meir's six-tefach ama, which the Rambam follows (Temidin 5:9). Set aside: R. Yehuda, for whom the Table is 10 × 5 tefachim and the loaf is turned up two and a half tefachim (Menachot 11:5). Adopted: uprights on the floor, for the one who sees the loaf as an open box; set aside: the loaf “like a rocking boat”, whose uprights rest on the Table (Menachot 94b). Tour's choice: the height of the uprights, which no source gives, and the incense cups set on the stacks, following the Sages; Abba Shaul (Menachot 11:5) and the Rambam (Beit HaBechirah 3:14; Temidin 5:2) place them beside the stacks.

mizbeach_hazahav.resume: The incense altar, at the center of the Heikhal between the Table and the Menora, slightly shifted toward the east. One ama by one ama, two amot high, in acacia wood gold-plated, with four horns and a rim. On Yom Kippur, the morning and evening incense is burned there as on every day; the incense proper to the day is burned in the Kodesh HaKodashim. On that day, this altar receives the blood sprinklings.
cotes: 1 × 1 ama × 2 high

The tour keeps the ordinary ama of six tefachim: 0.48 × 0.48 × 0.96 m.

parokhet.resume: In the First Temple, a wall one ama thick, the Amah Traksin, separated the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. In the Second, the Sages no longer knew whether this ama belonged to the Holy Place or to the Holy of Holies: so they hung TWO curtains, one ama apart, rather than decide. The outer curtain is fastened on the south, the inner one on the north: the Kohen Gadol enters from the south side, moves north along the one-ama space that separates them, and enters from the north — a path in an “S.” Each parokhet is 40 amot by 20, a tefach thick, woven of 72 threads of 24 strands, six of each of the four materials in equal parts: blue-purple, purple, scarlet and linen. No gold thread. The weave, ma'aseh choshev, bears a different image on each face — sometimes, Rashi explains, a lion on one side and an eagle on the other. Two new ones were made each year. From the Heikhal, one sees the ends of the bars of the Ark pressing the cloth, like two breasts.

parokhet.note: Adopted: the four materials — three wools and linen — are woven into every thread (Shekalim 8:5; Rashi on Exodus 26:31): the fabric is a mottled purple, not bands of color. Shmuel, however, counts this description among the three where the Sages speak “in exaggerated language” (Tamid 29a–b). Tour's choice: a heavy, flat fabric without drapery, and figures without any human face; the other image on the reverse side is not shown. Set aside: R. Yossi, for whom there was only a single parokhet (Yoma 5:1). Tour's choice: Yoma 54a speaks of only one parokhet; with two, the bars of the Ark cross the Amah Traksin, carry the inner curtain with them and make the outer one bulge.

kodesh_hakodashim.resume: The Holy of Holies: a room 20 amot by 20, under 40 amot of height, that is roughly 9.6 meters by 9.6 and 19 high. In the tour, no light enters it; the Kohen Gadol lights his way there by the embers of his fire-pan. At the center stands the Even HaShetiya, and on it the Ark. He sets the fire-pan of embers between the two bars of the Ark and stands there for the sprinklings. Only one person enters it for the service, one day of the year: the Kohen Gadol, at Kippur.

kodesh_hakodashim.note: Tour's choice: the stone and the Ark at the center of the room. Set aside: the Rambam, who places the stone “בְּמַעֲרָבוֹ”, in the western part of the Kodesh HaKodashim (Beit HaBechirah 4:1). Tour's choice: the darkness of the room, which no source describes.

even_hashetiya.resume: The foundation stone, at the center of the Kodesh HaKodashim: raw rock breaking through the gold floor, taken from the First Temple, and rising three fingers above it. The Ark rests on it.

even_hashetiya.note: Adopted: the stone at the center. Bava Batra 99a gives the Ark of Moses, in Shlomo's Temple, ten amot of space on every side; but this is a miracle — “מְקוֹם אָרוֹן וּכְרוּבִים אֵינוֹ מִן הַמִּדָּה” — and the baraita says nothing of the stone. Set aside: the Rambam, who places the stone in the western part of the Kodesh HaKodashim (Beit HaBechirah 4:1). Tour's choice: the irregular outline of the rock, its extent and its relief; only its height, three fingers, is fixed. First Temple: the gold floor (I Kings 6:30); Middot 4:1 speaks only of gold. In the Second Temple the stone stood empty, the Ark having been removed (Yoma 5:2); the tour shows the Temple to come, with the Ark resting on it.

aron.resume: The Ark of the Covenant, set on the Even HaShetiya. A chest 2.5 amot by 1.5 and 1.5 high, in acacia wood gold-plated inside and out — three nested chests, gold, wood, gold — the gold smooth, without any engraving. The outer gold chest is taller than the others: its rim rises around the lid and overtops it a little, like a crown, the keter Torah. Its long side is oriented north-south, its two bars, the badim, run east-west. Four gold rings are fixed at the upper corners, near the lid, two per side; the badim are never removed from them, and 2.5 amot separate them — enough to let two bearers pass between them. The Ark stays closed, always.

aron.note: Project's position: the tour shows the Temple to come, with the Ark in its place — the Ark of Moses, which Yoshiyahu hid (Yoma 52b; Rambam, Beit HaBechirah 4:1). No source describes its return, and Jeremiah 3:16 rather foretells that it will be forgotten: the Ark will no longer be spoken of, it will not come to mind, and no other will be made. Tour's choice: the smooth gold, without engraving, and the length of the poles, which no source gives; they cross the Amah Traksin, carry the inner curtain with them and press against the outer one, hence the bulges of Yoma 54a. Adopted: the rings at the upper corners (Rashi on Exodus 25:12). Set aside: the Ramban (on Exodus 25:12), who places them at the lower corners, and Ibn Ezra, who reads “פַּעֲמוֹתָיו” as feet.

kaporet.resume: The lid of the Ark: a plate of pure gold 2.5 amot by 1.5, a tefach thick — chest and lid together make ten tefachim. At its two ends, north and south, two keruvim, hammered out of the very mass of the lid: they rise from it, with no feet or base. They have a child's face, at least a tefach high, and measure ten tefachim. They are turned aside, toward each other and toward the House at once, like a pupil taking leave of his master, inclined toward the lid, wings spread at the level of the heads and a little above, without touching the body, forming a canopy over the kaporet.

kaporet.note: Adopted: keruvim with a child's face (Sukkah 5b; Rashi), a boy and a girl embracing. The tour applies to them the embrace of Yoma 54a–b, although the Gemara refers it to the First Temple or to cherubs drawn on the walls. Adopted: Onkelos's sideways faces (Bava Batra 99a, about Shlomo's keruvim), which reconcile “toward each other” (Exodus 25:20) and “toward the House” (II Chronicles 3:13). Set aside: faces turned now toward each other, now toward the House, according to Israel's conduct (Bava Batra 99a); the Rashbam's great birds (on Exodus 25:18). Tour's choice: no feet or base, and wings joined above the lid; Rashi says only that the keruvim are drawn out of its ends and that their wings rise near their heads (on Exodus 25:18 and 25:20). Not shown: Shlomo's standing keruvim, ten amot high (I Kings 6:23–28).

contenu_aron.resume: Four objects accompany the Ark. In front of it, between the badim, the jar of manna, of clay, and the staff of Aharon with its almonds and blossoms. Beside it, to the north, the chest that the Philistines sent back with it. The flask of anointing oil stands in front of it as well.

sources.citation: צְלוֹחִית שֶׁל חֶרֶס

contenu_aron.note: Adopted: in front of the Ark, only the manna and the staff (Rambam, Beit HaBechirah 4:1); the manna jar of clay, “צְלוֹחִית שֶׁל חֶרֶס” (Rashi on Exodus 16:33); the chest “beside” it (I Samuel 6:8; Bava Batra 14a). Tour's choice: the manna and the staff between the badim, the very place where the machta is set down (Yoma 5:1) — the Rambam only says “וּלְפָנָיו”; the place of the oil flask, which the sources only say was hidden with the Ark (Yoma 52b; Horayot 12a); and the north side for the chest. The Ark stays closed; neither the Tablets nor the Sefer Torah are visible. Set aside: the Sefer Torah placed beside the Ark, on the Philistines' chest or on a board, according to R. Yehuda (Bava Batra 14b).

machta.resume: The Yom Kippur fire pan, set down on the rock between the two poles, at the foot of the Ark. On that day it is of gold rather than silver, holds three kabin, is lighter than the everyday one, and its handle is long where the everyday one is short, so that the forearm carries its weight. The High Priest scooped the coals from the outer altar, carried the pan here in his right hand, set it down between the poles, then poured the incense onto the coals: the smoke fills the house. In the tour, these coals are the only light in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
cotes: three kabin, a light pan, a long handle
bowl 0.52 to 0.60 ama across, 0.16 high

sources.citation: בֵּין שְׁנֵי הַבַּדִּים

machta.note: The bowl, its handle and their measures are a CHOICE; its place between the poles, at the foot of the Ark, is Yoma 5:1. Tour's choice: the coals as the only light in the room, which no source describes. The High Priest carries it in his right hand despite the rule that would have it in the left: lighter than the everyday pan (Yoma 4:4), it is still too heavy and too hot for the left hand all the way to the Ark (Rambam, Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:1).
